options: A datastore that is not accessible from the external world because of technology barriers
A datastore that is only accessible to its relevant stakeholders
A datastore that stores data in a unified data model
A datastore used exclusively for decision support
A datastore that has been migrated to the cloud
questions.explanation: Unlike a Data Island, which is unreachable from outside, a Data Silo is a datastore accessible only to its relevant stakeholders.

questions.stem: How does a Data Island differ from a Data Silo?
options: A Data Island holds confidential data; a Data Silo never does
A Data Island is on-premises; a Data Silo is in the cloud
A Data Island is not accessible from the external world; a Data Silo is accessible only to relevant stakeholders
A Data Island is a process; a Data Silo is a technology
There is no difference; the two terms are interchangeable
questions.explanation: Data Islands cannot be reached from outside, often for technological reasons, whereas Data Silos are reachable but restricted to their relevant stakeholders.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT given as a reason why data ends up in a silo?
options: The datastore hosts confidential data such as finance or audit data
The data is semi-structured or unstructured and not readable
Data quality is so low that sharing it could lead to wrong decisions
The data has already been loaded into a data warehouse
Separate database instances are created for different development teams
questions.explanation: Confidentiality, unreadable formats, poor quality, security or privacy concerns and per-team development instances are all cited; loading data into a warehouse is the remedy, not a cause.

questions.stem: Why are separate database instances sometimes created for different development teams?
options: To reduce licensing costs
So that management can compare the teams' output
To enforce data privacy regulations
So that if one team changes data or table structures, other teams are not impacted
To increase query performance
questions.explanation: Per-team development instances isolate each team's data and structural changes so that they do not affect other teams.

questions.stem: Why should Data Silos not exist in a data-driven organisation?
options: Because they make the same kind of data impossible to correlate across systems
Because they consume too much storage
Because they are not permitted by database vendors
Because they are always hosted on legacy hardware
Because they cannot be encrypted
questions.explanation: If data does not reside in one location, it is not possible to correlate the same kind of data across multiple systems, which data scientists and management need.

questions.stem: Which problem did the Data Warehouse come into being to solve?
options: The lack of transaction processing capacity
Source-system data sitting in silos, making cross-departmental reporting slow and hard to validate
The absence of network connectivity between cities
The need to encrypt confidential finance data
The cost of cloud compute resources
questions.explanation: Data Warehousing brings data from all source systems into one place so management need not extract and validate data from each silo separately.

questions.stem: In Data Warehousing, in what form is data from all the source systems brought together?
options: As separate copies, one per department
As unstructured files in an object store
In a unified data model, forming a single source of truth for decision support
In per-team development instances
As a read-only Data Island
questions.explanation: Source data is consolidated into a unified data model so that Decision Support Systems have a single source of truth.

questions.stem: Which examples of siloed source systems does *I Am Datapedia!* say almost all medium to large organisations have?
options: Mainframe, Hadoop and Kafka
Data Lake, Data Mart and OLAP Cube
Tableau, Power BI and Qlik
Landing, Staging and Transformed zones
CRM, ERP, Procurement and HR systems
questions.explanation: The typical organisation has CRM, ERP, Procurement and HR systems, each holding its own data in a silo.

questions.stem: Which two difficulties arise when management wants information from several siloed systems?
options: Extraction is very time-consuming and data quality is hard to validate
Data encryption and data masking
Licensing and hardware procurement
Duplicate primary keys and missing indexes
Slow network links and limited RAM
questions.explanation: With data in silos, extracting it is time-consuming and validating its quality is difficult.

questions.stem: Which concepts describe the current era in which data silos are discouraged?
options: Per-team database instances
Data islands and floppy-drive transfers
Departmental ownership and restricted sharing
Manual reconciliation and canned reports
Data democratisation and data liberalisation as a norm
questions.explanation: The data-driven organisation not only centralises data but also makes data democratisation and liberalisation the norm.
